entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Decimus Carfulenus, referred to as Carsuleius by the historian Appian, was a dedicated Roman senator and military commander whose career was inextricably linked to the cataclysmic final decades of the Roman Republic. A staunch supporter of the senatorial cause, he found himself at the epicenter of the civil wars that followed Julius Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, steadfastly opposing Mark Antony and aligning with the faction championed by Cicero. His unwavering commitment to the Republic positioned him as a key, albeit ultimately tragic, figure in the power struggles that defined Rome's transition from a republican system to an imperial one, culminating in his death during the decisive Battle of Mutina in 43 BCE.

Carfulenus's military experience was honed during Caesar's Civil War, where he notably served under Julius Caesar himself during the Alexandrian War (48-47 BCE), achieving a position of command. However, with Caesar's death, his loyalties shifted dramatically. He unequivocally joined the republican forces, operating under the command of the consuls Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Vibius Pansa. In 43 BCE, as a consul-designate, Carfulenus was dispatched to Cisalpine Gaul to bolster the legions engaged in the siege of Mark Antony at Mutina. He played a critical role in the subsequent campaigns, fighting alongside Octavian and the consular armies, actively participating in several skirmishes and the main battle that ultimately broke Antony's siege.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Decimus Carfulenus played a direct, though ultimately fatal, role in the Battle of Mutina, a pivotal engagement that temporarily checked Mark Antony's power and set the stage for the Second Triumvirate. His death contributed to the high cost of the civil wars for the Roman Senate, weakening their ability to resist the rise of autocratic rule.
